subject: Cognitive Science
title: Decision Fatigue
description: A short lesson to help you apply Decision Fatigue.

hook.text: Israeli judges granted parole 65% of the time in the morning but nearly 0% right before lunch.

buildup.text: The decisions hadn't changed—the judges had. Their ability to decide well had drained over time.

discovery.text: Decision fatigue is real: each choice depletes a shared mental resource, making the next one worse.

twist.text: When depleted, people either choose the default option or avoid deciding at all.

climax.text: This is why Steve Jobs wore the same outfit daily. Eliminating trivial decisions preserves the resource.

punchline.text: Decisions are a budget. Spend them wisely.

quiz.question: What happens to decision quality over a long session?

details.summary: The quality of decisions deteriorates after a long session of decision-making. Judges grant parole more often after meals. Shoppers make worse choices late in the day. Decision fatigue depletes a finite cognitive resource, leading to impulsive or default choices when reserves run low.
details.whyItMatters: Decision fatigue explains why willpower fades and defaults win. Structuring when and how many decisions you face can meaningfully improve outcomes.
takeaways: Decision quality declines with the number of decisions made
Fatigue leads to impulsive choices or choosing the default
Scheduling important decisions early preserves cognitive resources

faq.question: What is the parole study that shows decision fatigue?
faq.answer: Israeli judges granted parole to about 65 percent of prisoners seen right after meals but nearly zero percent before meals. As decision fatigue accumulated, judges defaulted to the safer option of denying parole. Breaks and food replenished the cognitive resources needed for considered decisions.

faq.question: How can you reduce the impact of decision fatigue?
faq.answer: Make important decisions early in the day. Reduce trivial decisions through routines and habits. Batch similar decisions together. Use checklists and predetermined criteria to offload cognitive effort. Ensuring adequate food and rest also helps maintain decision quality.
